title: India's Egg Prices Hit Record Highs as Ethanol Push Squeezes Poultry Feed Supply
excerpt: Maize diversion to biofuel and soaring soybean costs create a twin feed shock, with retail prices up 40 percent and branded eggs expected to reach Rs 20-25
body:
• Egg prices have risen 35-40 percent year-on-year, with farm-gate prices at Rs 7 per egg and retail reaching Rs 8.50-9 — branded eggs could hit Rs 20-25 by winter
  • About 37 percent of India's 43.4 million-tonne maize crop — roughly 17 million tonnes — is now diverted to ethanol production, up from 1 million tonnes in 2022
  • The twin shock of surging maize and soybean meal costs has pushed egg production costs to Rs 5.20-5.50, prompting farmers to cull birds and cut chick placements

India's egg prices have climbed to record levels as the government's aggressive ethanol blending programme competes with the poultry industry for maize, the primary energy ingredient in chicken feed. Retail egg prices have surged 35 to 40 percent over the past year, and industry executives warn they could climb further as winter demand approaches.

Farm-gate prices have reached roughly Rs 7 per egg, according to the National Egg Coordination Committee (NECC), while retail prices are running at Rs 8.50-9 across major cities. In July, NECC's suggested monthly average prices were 23 to 39 percent higher year-on-year across all 34 centres it tracks, with Delhi recording a 38.7 percent increase.

The Ethanol-Maize Competition

At the centre of the price surge is India's ethanol blending mandate, which now requires oil marketing companies to blend petrol with 20 percent ethanol. The programme has rapidly expanded maize-based ethanol production from roughly 1 million tonnes in 2022 to more than 17 million tonnes today — consuming about 37 percent of India's total annual maize output of 43.4 million tonnes.

The diversion has sent maize prices from around Rs 14,000 per tonne three years ago to Rs 26,500 per tonne, a near-90 percent increase. Prices have jumped roughly 20 percent in just the past five months alone.

"Roughly 37% of the total maize production is now going to ethanol distilleries. In the past one year, egg prices have gone up by nearly 40% and are likely to rise further."

— Senior NECC official, to The Economic Times

Industry estimates suggest maize-based ethanol production could reach 25 million tonnes by 2030, intensifying the competition between fuel and food.

A Twin Feed Shock

Maize is not the only pressure point. Soybean meal — the key protein source in poultry feed — has surged more than 40 percent, from around Rs 45 per kilogram to Rs 65-66 per kilogram, amid tighter domestic soybean availability.

The combined cost increase has pushed egg production costs to Rs 5.20-5.50 per egg, up from Rs 4-4.50 earlier. Since maize and soybean meal together account for 60 to 70 percent of poultry production costs, farmers have limited room for substitution without affecting bird productivity.

Struggling with months of thin margins, many poultry farmers have responded by culling older hens prematurely and reducing fresh chick placements — decisions that will constrain egg supplies for months to come. Unlike broiler chicken, where supply can be adjusted relatively quickly, laying hens require months to mature before they begin producing eggs.

From Exporter to Importer

The tightening maize supply has also reshaped India's position in global grain markets. Once a significant exporter to Bangladesh and Vietnam, India imported a record 1 million tonnes of maize in FY25, bypassing normal trade quotas to source non-GMO grain from Myanmar and Ukraine. Current-year imports stand at roughly 500,000 tonnes, but industry executives expect volumes to rise further.

The poultry industry has called for a "feed-first principle" within the ethanol blending programme, arguing that livestock and poultry requirements should be met before fuel use claims available maize. Some industry leaders have also pushed for calibrated, trigger-based maize imports during periods of supply stress.

What It Means for Consumers

For Indian households where eggs are a primary protein source — particularly among lower and middle-income families — the price increase is significant. India produces roughly 130 billion eggs annually, and the NECC sets benchmark prices that ripple through the entire supply chain.

The picture is likely to worsen before it improves. Winter typically brings higher egg consumption, and branded eggs from suppliers like Eggoz and Country Chicken Co. are expected to reach Rs 20-25 per egg during peak months, according to leading Maharashtra distributors. Some relief may arrive when new kharif soybean and maize crops reach markets around October-November, but the structural shift of maize toward ethanol is expected to keep feed costs elevated above historical levels.

For the Indian diaspora, many of whom send remittances to families in India, rising food staple prices add to an already challenging household budget. Eggs remain among the cheapest animal protein sources available — but at Rs 9 retail, they cost nearly double what families paid just two years ago.
